summary: This RFC describes the BGP encodings and procedures for exchanging the information needed by multicast in MPLS/BGP IP VPNs, as specified in RFC 6513. It is the BGP side of the multicast VPN design.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the exact writing style routers use to tell each other about multicast groups in a private network. Following it means everyone's notes can be understood by everyone.

questions: what is the pmsi tunnel attribute
how does bgp carry multicast vpn join messages
subtitle: How BGP carries the routes, tunnel bindings and join messages that make multicast work across MPLS/BGP VPNs.

tldr.problem: Provider Edge routers in an MPLS/BGP IP VPN need a way to discover which sites belong to a multicast VPN, learn which provider tunnel carries each flow, and pass customer multicast joins to each other without running PIM between themselves.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6514 defines a new BGP address family (MCAST-VPN NLRI, SAFI 5) with seven route types, a PMSI Tunnel attribute, a Source AS and a VRF Route Import extended community, and a PE Distinguisher Labels attribute, plus procedures for using them.
tldr.outcome: It is the BGP half of the multicast VPN design in RFC 6513. It is a Proposed Standard, and thirteen later RFCs update it.

facts.label: Route types defined
facts.value: 7 (1 to 5 A-D routes, 6 and 7 C-multicast routes)

today: RFC 6514 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2012, and it has not been obsoleted. It has been updated by later RFCs, including RFC 6515, RFC 6625, RFC 7385 and RFC 10018, so read it together with those updates.

sections.title: What This RFC Adds to BGP
sections.content:
RFC 6514 describes the BGP encodings and procedures for exchanging the information that Multicast in MPLS/BGP IP VPNs needs, as specified in RFC 6513. It assumes thorough familiarity with that document.

It defines one new Network Layer Reachability Information type, the MCAST-VPN NLRI. It is used for MVPN auto-discovery, for advertising the binding of an MVPN to an Inclusive tunnel (I-PMSI), for binding a (C-S,C-G) flow to a Selective tunnel (S-PMSI), for exchanging customer multicast routing information among Provider Edge routers (PEs), for choosing a single forwarder PE, and for co-locating a customer rendezvous point on a PE.

It also specifies two new BGP attributes, the PMSI Tunnel attribute and the PE Distinguisher Labels attribute, and two new extended communities, Source AS and VRF Route Import.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers already have a language for sharing routes. This RFC teaches them a few new words so they can also share who wants which multicast stream.

sections.title: The MCAST-VPN NLRI and Its Route Types
sections.content:
Every MCAST-VPN NLRI starts with a one-octet Route Type and a one-octet Length that counts the route-type-specific part. The type selects the layout of the rest. Five types are auto-discovery (A-D) routes and two are C-multicast routes that carry customer join state.

The NLRI travels in the multiprotocol extensions of BGP with an AFI of 1 or 2 and a SAFI of MCAST-VPN. The AFI tells receivers whether the multicast source and group addresses inside are IPv4 (AFI 1) or IPv6 (AFI 2). Two speakers must agree through a BGP capabilities advertisement, using capability code 1 with that AFI and SAFI, before exchanging these routes.

Most layouts begin with an 8-octet Route Distinguisher. Where a source or group address appears, its length field is 32 for IPv4 or 128 for IPv6. Source Active A-D routes for groups in the Source Specific Multicast range MUST NOT be advertised and MUST be discarded if received.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message starts with a number that says what kind of message it is, like a form with a type box ticked at the top, and the rest of the form depends on which box is ticked.

sections.title: Tunnel Attribute, Communities and IANA Values
sections.content:
The PMSI Tunnel attribute is an optional transitive attribute with a flags octet, a tunnel type octet, a 3-octet MPLS label and a variable Tunnel Identifier. The only defined flag is Leaf Information Required (L). The tunnel type decides how the identifier is read. For example, an RSVP-TE P2MP LSP uses the fields of its SESSION object, and Ingress Replication carries the unicast endpoint address of the PE. A router treats the attribute as malformed if the tunnel type is undefined or the identifier cannot be parsed, and an implementation MUST log an error when that happens.

The Source AS extended community carries the ASN of the PE and a Local Administrator of 0. The VRF Route Import community carries an IP address of the PE and a 2-octet number that identifies the VRF, forming the C-multicast Import Route Target. A PE includes it on unicast VPN-IP routes that could be multicast sources or rendezvous points, so remote PEs know where to send joins. The PE Distinguisher Labels attribute is a list of PE address and label pairs.

IANA assigned SAFI 5 to MCAST-VPN and SAFI 129 to Multicast for BGP/MPLS IP VPNs. PMSI_TUNNEL is path attribute 22 and PE Distinguisher Labels is 27. The Source AS community is 0x0009 (two-octet AS-specific) and 0x0209 (four-octet), and VRF Route Import is 0x010b.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the stickers attached to a message. One says which truck to use, one says which company sent it, and one says which mailbox in the building it belongs to.

sections.title: Auto-Discovery and Tunnel Binding
sections.content:
A PE with a VRF of an MVPN originates an Intra-AS I-PMSI A-D route and advertises it in IBGP. The route carries the VRF's Route Distinguisher, the PE's address, and, when an inclusive tunnel is used, a PMSI Tunnel attribute naming the provider tree or the ingress replication endpoint. By default it carries the same export Route Targets as the VPN unicast routes, so any PE importing one of them treats the sender as a member of that MVPN. A receiving PE joins the advertised tree or uses the label and address for ingress replication. Several MVPNs may share one tree if the route also carries an MPLS upstream-assigned label.

When tunnels are segmented across autonomous systems, ASBRs also originate Inter-AS I-PMSI A-D routes, which aggregate the intra-AS routes into one route per AS and MVPN. An MVPN present in N ASes therefore needs N inter-AS tunnels, independent of the number of PEs. When a tree needs known leaves, the L flag asks receivers to answer with Leaf A-D routes. The text also describes a case where the multicast and unicast topologies differ, using a separate upstream-multicast-hop VRF with its own Route Targets.
sections.plainLanguage: Each office first announces that it is part of the newsletter club and which truck it will listen to. Border offices then bundle all the announcements from their country into one message for the next country.

sections.title: Exchanging Customer Join Information
sections.content:
When a PE learns of a customer join through PIM, it turns that state into a C-multicast route. A new (C-S,C-G) state whose upstream PE is not the local PE becomes a Source Tree Join route. A new (C-*,C-G) state becomes a Shared Tree Join route, with the C-RP address in the Multicast Source field. Deleting the state withdraws the route, which acts as a prune. When mLDP is the customer protocol, a Source Tree Join route is built from the root node address and opaque value.

To fill in the rest of the route, the PE finds the best upstream multicast hop route for the source. From it, the PE takes the upstream PE's AS for the Source AS field and the C-multicast Import Route Target from its VRF Route Import community, which becomes the Route Target of the join. The route reaches only that upstream PE. Because PIM messages are never sent from one PE to another, BGP carries all of this state.

Identical C-multicast routes for the same flow are aggregated by BGP itself, so a route reflector or an ASBR re-advertises only one of them. If a unicast routing change moves the upstream route for a source, the PE MUST re-originate its C-multicast routes.
sections.plainLanguage: When someone in an office says they want the newsletter from a certain sender, their post office sends one note straight to the post office closest to that sender, instead of shouting to everyone.

sections.title: Selective Tunnels and Source Active Routes
sections.content:
An S-PMSI A-D route binds one customer (C-S,C-G) flow to a provider tunnel of its own, so only interested PEs receive that flow. It carries the source, the group and a PMSI Tunnel attribute with the tunnel identity. Several selective tunnels may be aggregated onto one tree, and when they belong to different MVPNs the routes MUST carry an MPLS upstream-assigned label. An ASBR may merge upstream selective tunnels into a downstream inclusive one if a list of conditions holds, and it then MUST discard that flow's traffic received on the inclusive tunnel.

Two sections handle PIM sparse mode when customers move from a rendezvous-point tree to a source tree. If shared and source trees are both used between sites, a PE that gets a Source Tree Join originates a Source Active A-D route, and other PEs use it to prune that source off the shared tree, after a configurable timer so no PE is cut off early. If shared trees are not used between sites, the PE discovers active sources by acting as the customer RP or by learning them from Anycast-RP or MSDP, and floods Source Active routes so receivers can join the source directly.

A short section adds that the Carrier's Carrier model can be supported by using mLDP between the customer and provider edge.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes one popular newsletter gets its own truck so everyone else is not bothered. A Source Active message is like a sign that says, this sender is now sending, in case you want to switch to hearing from them directly.

sections.title: Scalability Measures
sections.content:
The RFC lists several ways to keep the control plane small. A PE should advertise its C-multicast Import Route Targets with a single Route Target Constraint, so each join reaches only the relevant PE, and intra-AS routes should carry the NO_EXPORT community. Aggregation at ASBRs means the number of inter-AS tunnels for an MVPN does not depend on the number of PEs.

Route reflectors can be partitioned among MVPNs, so no single reflector must hold routes for all of them, and they need not be the same ones used for VPN-IP routes. Both route reflectors and ASBRs keep C-multicast routes only in the control plane. Optional dampening, similar to the procedures of RFC 2439, can delay withdrawals of C-multicast routes and of Leaf A-D routes, and delay joins. Implementations SHOULD allow the delay to be configured, and support for dampening of withdrawals is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: To keep the post offices from drowning in notes, they pack many notes into one, send each note only to who needs it, and sometimes wait a moment before announcing that someone has left.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanisms can reuse existing BGP security. Provider-provisioned VPN threats are discussed in RFC 4111, and additional multicast threats in RFC 6513. The text says the TCP Authentication Option of RFC 5925 SHOULD be used where authentication of BGP control packets is needed.

A PE MUST NOT accept routes with the MCAST-VPN SAFI from CEs. If BGP is the CE-PE protocol and a route from a CE carries the VRF Route Import community, the PE MUST remove it, and routes advertised to a CE MUST NOT carry it. To stop one VPN from hogging PE resources, implementations SHOULD allow rate limiting of BGP messages used for C-multicast routes, and an upper bound on the number and frequency of S-PMSI A-D routes and, in some modes, Source Active A-D routes, per PE and per MVPN.
sections.plainLanguage: A customer must never be allowed to send these special notes into the provider's network, and nobody should be allowed to use up all the post office's time with too many notes.

items.label: Intra-AS I-PMSI A-D
items.desc: A PE announces its VRF and inclusive tunnel inside its AS.

items.label: Inter-AS I-PMSI A-D
items.desc: An ASBR announces an AS-level inclusive tunnel to other ASes.

items.label: S-PMSI A-D
items.desc: Binds a (C-S,C-G) flow to a selective tunnel.

items.label: Leaf A-D
items.desc: Reply that tells a tunnel root who its leaves are.

items.label: No tunnel information
items.desc: Used to track a flow without binding it to a provider tunnel.

items.label: RSVP-TE P2MP LSP
items.desc: Identifier follows the RSVP-TE P2MP SESSION object.

items.label: mLDP P2MP LSP
items.desc: Identifier is a P2MP FEC element.

items.label: PIM-SSM Tree
items.desc: Identifier is a P-root node address and P-multicast group.

items.label: PIM-SM Tree
items.desc: Identifier is a sender address and P-multicast group.

items.label: BIDIR-PIM Tree
items.desc: Identifier is a sender address and P-multicast group.

items.label: Ingress Replication
items.desc: Identifier is the PE's unicast tunnel endpoint address.

items.label: mLDP MP2MP LSP
items.desc: Identifier is an MP2MP FEC element.
